title: Rate limits & org/project keys demo with Northstar Health
summary: Redwood AE/SE demo of org/project keys, per-project rate limits, quotas and multi-tenant controls. Customer is evaluating options for dev->prod migration with VPC and strict tenancy controls. Agreed to run a short POC and send security docs and pricing.
topics: org/project keys, per-project rate limits, token quotas, burst capacity, dedicated vs hosted, security controls (SSO, KMS), billing separation
next_steps: Tom to share rate limits deck and pricing spreadsheet by 2026-03-16
Maya to provision demo tenant and send invite for POC baseline tests (throughput + latency) by 2026-03-18
Nina to review SOC2 + encryption docs and confirm any additional controls by 2026-03-20
action_items: Tom Ellis - Share rate limits deck + org/project keys doc - 2026-03-16
Maya Chen - Setup demo tenant and sample project keys, run baseline against their test harness - 2026-03-18
Nina Rao - Confirm security follow-ups (KMS, HSM, SSO) - 2026-03-20
transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-03-14 16:00 PDT
Duration: 45 minutes
Attendees: Tom Ellis (Redwood AE), Maya Chen (Redwood SE), Ravi Patel (Redwood CSM); Jorge Alvarez (Northstar Eng), Leah Kim (Northstar Product), Nina Rao (Northstar Security)

[00:00] Tom (Redwood AE): Hey everyone thanks for joining, uh this is Tom from Redwood, with Maya our solutions engineer and Ravi from success. How's everyone doing?
[00:06] Jorge (Northstar): Good, thanks. We, uh, we got a 45 minute slot so let's try to keep things tight. We're mainly interested in how you do org-level rate limits and project keys — we have multi-tenant constraints.
[00:18] Tom: Perfect. Quick agenda: we'll demo the Console for org/project keys, show how per-project quotas and rate limits work, talk about billing separation and security controls, then Q&A and next steps. Sound good?
[00:28] Leah: Yep, that works.
[00:30] Maya (Redwood SE): Cool. I will share my screen now — bear with me while the deck loads.
[00:37] [screen share begins]
[00:40] Maya: Alright so first up, this is the Redwood Console. On the left you'll see Organization -> Projects -> Keys. For Northstar we'd recommend creating one org for the company, then a project for each product line or environment (dev/prod). Each project gets its own set of API keys.
[01:00] Jorge: And those keys can be scoped? Like read-only vs generate? We need fine-grained controls for different teams.
[01:06] Maya: Yes, keys are role-scoped; currently we support project-admin, project-user and read-only, and you can restrict by endpoint as well - so a key could be allowed embeddings but not generation, or allowed to call a low-rate reranker endpoint only.
[01:20] Nina (Security): Can you tie keys to our SSO/SCIM users? We want auditability and ability to rotate keys automatically.
[01:26] Maya: Good question. We integrate with SAML/SSO so users map to Redwood RBAC roles. Keys themselves can be created by a user or by the system for service accounts; we store key creation audit data, and rotation is supported via the Console or API.
[01:40] [01:42] Tom: Jumping to rate limits: we have per-project quotas (monthly token quotas), and per-project rate limits (tokens/sec or requests/sec) with burst settings.
[01:52] Leah: How does burst capacity work? We have spiky traffic from certain clinics at 9am local.
[01:58] Maya: We implement a token-bucket model. Each project has a steady allowed rate and a bucket for bursts up to configured size. We also have org-level fallbacks: if one project exceeds its quota and we can't serve, requests can either be throttled, queued briefly, or routed to a lower-cost compatible model if you've configured fallbacks.
[02:18] Jorge: Wait, routed to a compatible model automatically? Can that be turned off?
[02:21] Maya: Absolutely — you configure routing policies per project. Default is no automatic model fallback unless you opt in.
[02:28] [02:30] Jorge: For compliance we prefer explicit throttling rather than automatic model switching.
[02:33] Maya: Totally understandable, you can set the policy to drop/429 or queue with max wait. We show SLO metrics in the console so you can see throttled vs served rates.
[02:44] Nina: How do you handle billing separation? We need separate cost reporting per project and per team, with monthly quotas enforced.
[02:52] Tom: Billing is tied to projects; you can enable per-project billing export to S3 or our billing API. Quotas can be configured in tokens per month and the Console will prevent new requests when quota exhausted, or you can set up overage rules and alerts.
[03:06] Leah: Is that token calc aligned with our existing tokenization? We use a mixture of short prompts + long context in some workflows.
[03:12] Maya: We show token estimation per model; for project quotas you set token units and we bill/charge on tokens consumed. There is an option to count only prompt tokens or total tokens depending on contract but the default is total tokens.
[03:24] [03:25] Ravi (Redwood CSM): Many customers keep a conservative quota on dev projects to avoid surprises, then bump for prod.
[03:30] Jorge: Makes sense. For POC we'd like a dev project with a 50k token monthly quota and stricter rate limit, then a prod project where burst is allowed.
[03:40] Maya: Perfect — we can preconfigure that in the demo tenant.
[03:44] [03:46] Maya: Now switching to API — keys are passed in Authorization header as usual. For org/project keys we also accept a project header (x-redwood-project) or you can embed the project in the key itself (project-scoped key) so requests are automatically attributed.
[03:58] Jorge: If someone mistakenly uses a project key against a different project, is that prevented?
[04:02] Maya: Keys are cryptographically bound to the project. If used elsewhere the request is rejected. There are also rate-limit windows applied at the project ID level, so even if a key leaks it can't exceed the project limits.
[04:15] Nina: On the security side, we need to know where keys live — are they stored encrypted with a customer KMS? 
[04:21] Maya: By default keys are encrypted using Redwood-managed KMS, but for Private customers or Dedicated we support customer-managed keys (bring-your-own KMS / HSM). We can include that in the Private offering or an enterprise add-on.
[04:34] Leah: For a multi-tenant product, can we have both shared model endpoints and isolated per-tenant pools? We want isolation for PHI-heavy tenants.
[04:43] Tom: Yes. You can run a hybrid: most tenants hit the shared hosted pool with rate limits and project keys, while PHI tenants get Dedicated capacity or Private deployment in a VPC for data isolation. We also have routing policies to route specific projects to dedicated pools.
[04:58] Jorge: How much latency overhead does the routing add?
[05:01] Maya: Negligible — routing is a policy decision at the edge. If it's a different pool there is the usual network hop; for Dedicated the latency profile is predictable and we provide benchmarks.
[05:12] [05:15] Jorge: Can we test that in a POC? Run 95th percentile latency and a burst test.
[05:18] Tom: Yes, that's part of the POC checklist. We'll do baseline throughput and a 5-minute burst test to confirm rate limit behavior and queueing.
[05:26] [05:28] Maya: I'll demo the Console limit config now. Here is a project config panel — you can set 'requests per minute', 'tokens per minute', monthly quota, and burst size. You can also set a throttle action: reject, queue (with max wait), or fallback to model variant.
[05:46] [06:00] Maya: Example: Project 'northstar-dev' — requests/min 60, tokens/min 10k, burst 20k, monthly 50k. When the bucket is empty requests return 429 with a Retry-After or you can set a webhook to notify.
[06:18] Leah: Do you offer per-route limits? For example restrict the /generate endpoint to 10 r/s but allow /embeddings higher?
[06:25] Maya: Yes, per-route limits are supported. In practice customers use route-level limits to protect expensive model calls while allowing higher throughput for embeddings or rerankers.
[06:36] [06:40] Jorge: What about API keys for internal apps vs external partners? We need partner keys with stricter quotas and IP allowlisting.
[06:47] Maya: You can create project-scoped partner keys and add IP allowlists. Also keys can be flagged as partner keys so they appear in separate billing buckets.
[06:56] Nina: How are audit logs surfaced? We need immutable logs, retention policy, and log export.
[07:03] Tom: We keep per-request logs (metadata only — we avoid storing full prompt text unless configured). Audit logs can be exported to your S3 or to a SIEM. Retention policies are configurable; longer retention is part of the enterprise compliance package.
[07:18] Nina: What about encryption in transit and at rest?
[07:21] Maya: TLS 1.2+ in transit, and at rest we encrypt keys and logs. For customer-managed KMS we can wrap stored secrets with your KMS.
[07:30] [07:32] Jorge: Any differences in how rate limits are enforced in Redwood Hosted vs Redwood Dedicated vs Private?
[07:36] Maya: Core enforcement logic is the same. In Hosted we operate a global control plane that enforces limits and applies routing. In Dedicated the control plane can be in the customer VPC or connected in a hybrid model; enforcement happens at the serving edge to avoid hops. In Private (air-gapped) you run the entire control plane and enforcement locally. Some features like org-level cross-project aggregations require connectivity in hybrid setups but we can support offline mode with periodic reconciles.
[08:00] Leah: We currently have an infra team that runs Seldon-based endpoints; they push back on adding another layer that might complicate their observability.
[08:09] Tom: Totally — we integrate with common observability stacks (Prometheus, Grafana, Datadog). You can export per-project metrics, traces, token usage and latencies to your existing stack.
[08:18] Jorge: Are there rate-limit metrics per-key as well?
[08:21] Maya: Yes, you can drill down from org -> project -> key and see usage, throttles, and recent request samples (metadata).
[08:30] [08:32] Nina: One more security detail: for PCI/PHI we need proof of separation — can you provide architecture diagrams and SOC2 evidence?
[08:39] Tom: Yes, we'll include SOC2 cert and architecture docs in the follow-up packet. For PHI we recommend Dedicated or Private and we'll detail the network and encryption architecture.
[08:50] [08:55] Maya: Quick live demo of setting a per-route limit: I'm setting /generate to 5 r/s and /embeddings to 50 r/s for project northstar-test... saving... Now I'll run a local script to simulate traffic. (background typing)
[09:10] [09:30] Maya: You'll see the console graph — requests spike and anything above 5 r/s on /generate gets 429 and shows up in the throttled bucket; embeddings continue to flow.
[09:40] Jorge: Looks good. In the logs can we see the 429 reason and the configured policy?
[09:44] Maya: Yes, the response includes a structured error code like RBW_RATE_LIMIT_EXCEEDED and Retry-After. The console stores the policy version that triggered it.
[09:52] Lee (sic) Speaker 1: (crosstalk)
[09:55] Leah: Sorry, just confirming: can we set different quotas per region? Some of our EU tenants require data residency and separate quotas.
[10:02] Maya: You can scope projects to regions; quotas and keys are regionalized. For EU data residency we recommend spinning a dedicated EU project backed by EU regions or using Private deployment.
[10:14] Jorge: On the POC, we want a test that shows: 1) per-project token quota enforcement, 2) per-route throttle behavior, 3) queuing vs drop behavior, 4) billing export correctness.
[10:26] Tom: We'll run that. We'll also capture 95th/99th latency and show SLO graphs.
[10:32] [10:35] Maya: For the demo tenant I'll provision two projects: northstar-dev (50k monthly tokens, strict rps) and northstar-prod (500k tokens, burst allowed). We'll also create a partner project with IP allowlist and a partner key.
[10:48] Nina: Please ensure logs do not contain PII in the sample requests. We will run with scrubbed payloads during the POC.
[10:55] Maya: Understood. By default we store metadata only; if you want full logs we can enable them but it's controlled by your contract.
[11:02] [11:05] Tom: Pricing question — what happens if a project goes over quota? Does it auto-bill?
[11:09] Maya: We support both models: hard cutoffs (reject until next period) or soft overage with per-token overage pricing. That is configurable per-org.
[11:18] Leah: We prefer alerts + delayed overage so apps don't break unexpectedly.
[11:22] Tom: Ok we'll recommend soft overage for critical services and hard for dev projects.
[11:26] [11:28] Jorge: Any integration with our internal rate limiters or API gateway? We might prefer to enforce some limits upstream.
[11:34] Maya: You can do hybrid enforcement — upstream gateway does coarse throttling and Redwood enforces fine-grained per-project/route quotas. Plus you get observability and aggregated billing.
[11:44] [11:50] (discussion about SLA & support tiers)
[11:50] Tom: For Dedicated we have SLA-backed latency and uptime; Private comes with enterprise support. We'll include SLA matrix in the follow-up.
[11:58] Nina: Will you include a data flow diagram showing where tokens, logs, and keys live?
[12:02] Tom: Yes, that will be included.
[12:05] [12:08] (final Q&A and recap)
[12:10] Tom: Quick recap: we'll provision a demo tenant, two projects, sample keys, run the POC tests (quota enforcement, burst tests, latency), send SOC2 and architecture docs, and pricing spreadsheet.
[12:20] Leah: Timeline?
[12:22] Tom: We'll send docs by EOD 2026-03-16, demo tenant and initial creds by 2026-03-18, POC test window week of 03-22.
[12:30] Jorge: Sounds good. Thanks folks.
[12:32] Tom: Thanks everyone. We'll follow up in email with links to the deck and the demo sign-up.

References:
- Deck: link (shared) - "Redwood rate limits & org keys.pdf"
- Demo tenant URL: will be shared in follow-up
- Security docs: SOC2, KMS options (attached)

Action items (reiterated):
- Tom: Send rate limit deck + pricing spreadsheet (2026-03-16)
- Maya: Provision demo tenant, create northstar-dev and northstar-prod projects, generate keys (2026-03-18)
